title: Data
text:
When the quantity of interest is unobserved, I build the data. Every paper ships with a journal-grade replication archive; the datasets below are released, or built for release, as standalone public resources.
Malaysia Election Panel Data, 1959–2018. A constituency-level panel covering every Malaysian general election, built from primary electoral records with boundary harmonization across successive redistricting exercises. Available at Zenodo.
Lower Chamber Elections Archive, Malaysia. Contributed to the Constituency-Level Elections Archive (CLEA), including candidate-, district-, and party-coding corrections fed back to the archive.
Three-Country Candidate Career Panels. Career-trajectory panels for every dominant-party candidate in three regimes: the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) in Malaysia (1959–2022), the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) in Japan (1947–2014), and the Kuomintang (KMT) in Taiwan (1986–2024), assembled from primary records in three languages with documented codebooks. Public release planned alongside the associated paper, “Crisis from Within.”
Geocoded Settlement Layers for Peninsular Malaysia. Geocoded layers of Emergency-era Chinese New Villages and Federal Land Development Authority (FELDA) schemes, joined to historical constituency boundaries for every delineation since 1955, with census-interpolated ethnic composition. Released through the replication archives of the associated papers.

title: Tyler Rongxuan Chen
text:
Hi, I’m Tyler! Welcome to my website.

I am a Ph.D. candidate in Political Science and Scientific Computing at the University of Michigan, where I am also completing an M.A. in Statistics. I study the relationship between political parties and the populations beneath them. Party systems stand on social groups, and I ask what happens when the groups move. My work combines comparative politics, with a focus on dominant parties and communal politics in Southeast and East Asia, and political methodology, with a focus on ecological inference. I read my cases in Chinese, Malay, and Indonesian.
My dissertation, “Moving Ground: Three Papers on Elites, Voters, and the Breakdown of Dominant Party Systems,” asks how parties that dominated their countries’ politics for decades lose the ability to dominate. Breakdown, I argue, takes two forces meeting. Populations shift beneath the party, and defecting elites attach their new vehicles to the ground that has moved. One paper shows the ground moving in Malaysia, where urbanization dissolved the brokered ties binding Chinese voters to the ruling coalition while the constitutionally entitled Malay base held. A second follows 4,638 candidate-elections across Malaysia’s UMNO, Japan’s LDP, and Taiwan’s KMT to show that defection ends dominance only when a breakaway party captures a social cleavage the parent cannot absorb. A third builds BACH, a simulation-based ecological-inference framework that recovers how each demographic subgroup votes from aggregate election returns, and finds that national origin rather than education organizes Hispanic vote choice in Florida.
The plan is for the dissertation to grow into a book, “The Tower of Babel We Bury.” The dissertation takes the groups as given and shows how their movement breaks parties. The book asks where the groups came from. Parties do not merely mobilize social groups. They make them, and campaigning on a made group means burying the differences inside it. The book follows buried difference from its colonial origins to its resurfacing across Malaysia, Taiwan, and the United States. My fieldwork runs from the Malay neighborhoods of Kuala Lumpur and the coastal villages of Terengganu to the Detroit suburbs and New York City’s three Chinatowns.
My research appears in the Journal of East Asian Studies and, with Congcong Fu, in the two leading Chinese-language journals of Southeast Asian studies. Three further papers are under review. I study what happens when the ground beneath a party shifts, and I build the instruments to measure it.
My papers, datasets, and CV are linked above.
I am on the 2026–27 academic job market.
Outside the academy, I am the dad of two black cats, Erik and Theda, and a volunteer foster with the Humane Society of Huron Valley.

title: Teaching
text: I am prepared to teach the quantitative methods sequence at every level — from introductory statistics through regression, causal inference, and Bayesian and computational methods — as well as courses on political parties, elections, democratization, and East and Southeast Asian politics.

title: Research
text:
What lies behind the change of political parties and party systems? I study both the elite origins and the societal foundations of parties and party systems, and I build the ecological-inference tools that recover how groups actually vote from aggregate election results and censuses.
My dissertation, “Moving Ground: Three Papers on Elites, Voters, and the Breakdown of Dominant Party Systems,” argues that dominant parties fall when two forces meet. Populations shift beneath the party, and defecting elites attach their new vehicles to the ground that has moved. Three papers below carry the argument. “Written on the Soil” shows the ground moving in Malaysia. “Crisis from Within” follows the elites who convert the movement into breakdown across Malaysia, Japan, and Taiwan. “What Race and Ethnicity Hide” builds BACH, the ecological-inference framework the first two require, and validates it against voter-file ground truth in the United States.
The plan is for the dissertation to grow into a book, “The Tower of Babel We Bury: Geography, Group-Making, and the Communal Foundations of Party Systems.” The dissertation takes the groups as given and shows how their movement breaks parties. The book asks where the groups came from, how parties bury the differences inside them, and what happens when buried difference resurfaces. It develops the argument across Malaysia, Taiwan, and the United States, with fieldwork running from the Malay neighborhoods of Kuala Lumpur to New York City’s three Chinatowns. “Legible Domains,” under review below, carries the book’s colonial-origins material.
Because these questions outrun existing tools, I also build new ones. I work on ecological inference that recovers group behavior from aggregate returns, spatial models for electorates whose boundaries move, and corrections for measurement error in demographic panels. The flagship is BACH, a simulation-based ecological-inference estimator that recovers subgroup voting behavior where survey nonresponse, partisan polarization, and cross-cutting cleavages defeat conventional tools.

title: Research
text:
Peer-Reviewed Publications
“Myth and Measurement: Spatial Heterogeneity, Ecological Fallacy, and the Urban Narrative in Peninsular Malaysia’s Electoral Politics.” 2026. Journal of East Asian Studies 26(1): 87–112. [Open Access] [Replication]
Does Malaysia vote along urban–rural lines or along ethnic ones? Combining aggregate election returns from Peninsular Malaysia with survey evidence and modeling spatial heterogeneity to guard against ecological fallacy, the paper shows that the celebrated urban–rural divide is largely an artifact of aggregation: ethnicity, not urbanization, remains the dominant cleavage structuring party competition. The result demonstrates that aggregate election data, analyzed with attention to spatial heterogeneity, can substitute for surveys in settings where reliable polling is scarce.
“Social Transformation in Malaysia and the Fragmentation of the Malay-Dominant Political Parties: Based on a Social Cleavage Structure Theory Perspective” (with Congcong Fu). Southeast Asian Studies (东南亚研究) 2021(3): 1–29. In Chinese. [Chinese Full Text] [English Translation on SSRN]
After Malaysia’s 2018 general election, five Malay-dominant parties held federal seats from Peninsular Malaysia alone, all tracing back to successive splits from UMNO. Drawing on social cleavage structure theory, the article argues that the fragmentation of Malay-dominant parties is the joint product of elite contradictions within political society and shifting cleavage structures within civil society. When intra-elite conflicts cannot be reconciled, or when a new social cleavage emerges, a new party is born; its survival depends on whether it can anchor itself to an existing or newly formed cleavage.
“Social Transformation, Dispute over Routes and the Split of Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS)” (with Congcong Fu). Southeast Asian Affairs (南洋问题研究) 2020(1): 79–95. In Chinese. [Chinese Full Text] [English Translation on SSRN]
The expansion of the Malay ethnic middle class and the imbalance of regional development weakened the Ulama faction and differentiated the professional group within the Malaysian Islamic Party (PAS), triggering a dispute over how to realize an Islamic state. The internal struggle culminated in the 2015 split that produced the National Trust Party (AMANAH). The article traces this process through the changing factional composition of PAS and argues that AMANAH’s long-term survival requires differentiated positioning relative to other Malay-based parties and a unified ideological foundation.

title: Research
text:
Under Review
“The Front Page and the Back Room: Demand Narrowing, Elite Coordination, and the Survival of Authoritarian Elites.”
When an authoritarian leader faces a crisis they may not survive, how does a divided elite coordinate on abandoning them before the moment passes? The paper argues that two features of the crisis resolve the elite’s coordination problem: a public signal that narrows the opposition’s demand onto the leader by name, making their removal a survivable exit, and a communication environment open enough for divided elites to read that narrowing as common knowledge. Where both hold, the elite sheds the leader and keeps its places; where the demand stays systemic, or never settles on a target, the elite closes ranks and the leader endures. A global-game model carries the mechanism, tested at two scales: a day-by-day reconstruction of the week of Soeharto’s fall in May 1998, coded daily across twenty-seven elites in two dailies, and a seven-crisis comparison that separates leader-removal from elite survival on the same two features. The leader falls; the elite survives.
“Legible Domains: Colonial Rule, Social Density, and the Forms of Communal Politics in Malaysia and Indonesia.”
Part of the book project, “The Tower of Babel We Bury.”
Why do some communal institutions survive decades of hostile policy while comparable ones next door are extinguished? Comparing Malaysia and Indonesia through comparative-historical analysis, the paper argues that two parameters set the terrain. One is a community’s social density. The other is whether the colonial state chose to register, codify, or spatially contain it. Malaysian Chinese society, above all its Chinese-language school system, was among the densest communal spheres under British Malaya yet among the least regulated, leaving the post-colonial state facing a community with the societal roots to push back. These colonial-era choices still shape where governments can and cannot break the communities that vote against them.
“Symbolic Power and the Functional Divide: Campaigns Across the Party-State Spectrum.”
Regimes differ in how fully the ruling party absorbs the state it governs, a range the paper calls the party-state spectrum. Across that spectrum, recurrent mobilizational campaigns are the instrument by which a party keeps the state it built subordinate to political ends. Drawing on seven decades of the Chinese party press, firm-level event studies that estimate campaigns’ economic impact, and daily social-media discourse, the paper documents campaigns’ functional logic: they discipline the state apparatus and renew the party’s symbolic authority over it.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers
“Written on the Soil: Why Urbanization Broke Only Half of a Dominant-Party Regime.” [SSRN]
The first paper of my dissertation, “Moving Ground.”
Where “Myth and Measurement” shows that ethnicity, not urbanization, remains Malaysia’s master cleavage, this paper shows how urbanization still mattered, working through the ethnic cleavage rather than against it. Whether urbanization threatens an electoral authoritarian regime depends on institutions the regime itself built: the state-made geography of ethnic groups, and the form of each group’s distributive incorporation. A group incorporated through brokered exchange is tied to place, because benefits flow through settlements and their brokers, and cities dissolve both; a group held by an entitlement attached by law to membership loses nothing when its members move. Using ecological inference, a settlement-level event study, and survey evidence across 1974–2018 in Malaysia, the paper shows that Chinese support collapsed where cities grew, while the constitutionally entitled Malay base held until an intra-Malay elite rupture. Exclusion did not doom the regime; it decided which coalition could bring it down.
“Crisis from Within: Elite Defection, Intraparty Competition, and the Breakdown of Dominant Party Systems.” [SSRN]
The second paper of my dissertation, “Moving Ground.”
When and how do dominant party systems break? The cracks they do not recover from come from within, after years of electoral dominance, opened by the party’s most successful politicians rather than its marginal ones. Across 4,638 candidate-elections in Malaysia’s UMNO (1959–2018), Japan’s LDP (1958–1993), and Taiwan’s KMT (1986–2001), a monopoly over office forces losing elites to choose between marginalization and exit, producing bloc exits, when cohesive factions leave together after losing leadership struggles, and marginal exits, when weakened candidates depart alone. Whether a split actually ends the party’s dominance is downstream: breakaway parties endure only when they attach to a social cleavage the parent cannot absorb. Breakdown is an elite phenomenon in its onset and a cleavage phenomenon in its consequences.
“What Race and Ethnicity Hide: Bayesian Approximate Computation with Hierarchical Framework (BACH) for Subgroup Voting Behavior under Partisan Polarization, Cross-Cutting Cleavages, and Survey Nonresponse.” [SSRN] [Poster at PolMeth 2026]
The third paper of my dissertation, “Moving Ground.”
A simulation-based ecological-inference framework that recovers subgroup voting behavior from aggregate election returns under the three conditions that defeat existing tools simultaneously: partisan polarization, cross-cutting cleavages, and survey nonresponse. The framework is validated through large-scale simulation experiments and benchmarked against Florida voter-file ground truth that reveals individual-level vote choice. Substantively, national origin rather than education organizes Hispanic vote choice, a within-race cleavage that conventional race-level ecological estimators collapse.
“Research Note: A Higher-Order Method of Moments Approach to Ecological Inference under Extreme Survey Nonresponse.” [SSRN]
When surveys are unreliable or absent, as in historical elections and many democracies without polling infrastructure, how can we recover who votes for whom? This research note derives a method-of-moments estimator that exploits higher-order moments of the cross-unit distribution of aggregate election outcomes to identify group voting behavior without individual-level data, offering a closed-form alternative to simulation-based approaches.
“What the Slope Loses, the Intercepts Gain: Measurement Error and Misattributed Effects in Fixed- and Random-Effects Models” (with Robert Franzese). [Latest Draft]
Fixed- and random-effects models compare each unit to itself over time. When a treatment moves slowly but its measure carries fast-moving error, the within transformation strips out the signal and keeps the noise, and the effect it loses does not simply attenuate; it migrates into the unit intercepts, masquerading as stable “unit characteristics.” Larger samples make this worse, tightening confidence intervals around the wrong value and driving the Hausman test toward the most biased specification. The paper proves the result, establishes a scope condition (unit effects worsen attenuation only when the signal is more persistent than the error), and supplies a diagnose–correct–redesign protocol validated on three datasets.
“Plant Closures and Trump-Related Twitter Discussion: A Spatial-Temporal Description” (with Robert Franzese). [Latest Draft]
How do local economic shocks shape online political extremism? Using a national geocoded tweet corpus matched to plant-closure events across the United States, the paper traces how local plant-closure shocks shaped Trump-related and extremist engagement on social media, mapping the spatial and temporal diffusion of economic-grievance discourse.
